transcript.content: Hi, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came in because my mind keeps… blanking out, I guess. Like at work, I’ll be looking right at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I can’t remember the steps I’ve done for years. It’s embarrassing, because that job is all about paying attention, and I used to know the routine like making coffee—well, I don’t even make it the same way every day, my sister says I put too much creamer in it—but with the road stuff, it’s serious. I just freeze and can’t think.
Did this start after something very upsetting or frightening happened to you?

Yeah… it did. I mean, I think that’s when it really started—after my closest friend died. That was about… a year and eight months ago now, which is strange because I still count it by months sometimes, like I’m keeping track of something. We used to talk about the dumbest things, grocery store music and whether birds know when it’s raining before people do, and then after she was gone, everything kind of… shifted. So, yes, after that.
Have you had times when you couldn’t remember important personal information about yourself, not just the steps of a task?

I don’t… I don’t think so. Not like my name or where I live or anything like that, if that’s what you mean. I mean, sometimes I’ll walk into a room and forget why I’m there, but my sister says everybody does that, especially if you’re carrying laundry and thinking about the grocery list at the same time.

Important personal information… I guess I’m not sure what counts. I haven’t noticed big pieces of myself missing, no. It’s more like I get stuck on what I’m supposed to be doing right then.
When your mind goes blank at work, do you feel intensely worried right then?

I’m not sure if it’s worry exactly. I mean, I don’t stand there thinking, “I’m worried,” it’s more like everything gets… quiet and jammed up. Then afterward I think about it a lot, like what if I missed something, or if someone noticed.

But right in the moment? I don’t know. It’s hard to separate, because the cars are there and the signs, and sometimes there’s that smell from the asphalt when it’s hot, and my gloves never fit right. So I know something is happening, but I don’t know if “intensely worried” is the right word.
When your mind goes blank, does the world around you ever feel unreal or dreamlike?

I’m not sure… dreamlike is a hard word for me. Sometimes when I’m standing there it feels like I’m not catching up with what’s happening, like the cars and people are moving and I’m a second behind, but I don’t know if that means unreal.

It’s not like in movies where everything goes wavy or anything. I mostly notice little things, like the pole feeling too heavy or the beeping from a truck backing up, and then I’m thinking about how those beeps sound like the microwave my mom had when I was a kid, which is… not helpful when I’m supposed to be watching traffic. So, I guess I haven’t really thought of it as the world feeling dreamlike.
When your mind goes blank, do memories or images of your friend’s death suddenly come into your mind?

I don’t know… not exactly like that. I mean, I know what you’re asking, I think, like if a picture of it just pops in, but when my mind goes blank it’s more like there’s nothing there for a second.

Sometimes a random thing will remind me of other random things, like a sound or the way the light hits the road, and then I’m off thinking about something else. Like yesterday there was this crow sitting on the sign, and I started thinking about how smart crows are and how my neighbor used to feed them peanuts. But I haven’t really noticed memories or images of my friend’s death coming in right then, no.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

Yeah… most days, I think. Especially in the mornings. I wake up and there’s this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, like the day is already wrecked before I’ve even gotten out of bed.

It’s strange because the room can look the same, the curtains and the little crack in the ceiling I keep meaning to fix, and I’ll think about needing to buy spackle, and then I’m just lying there feeling like… what’s the point of starting. So yes, down. Depressed, I guess, most mornings and a lot of days.
Have you been feeling depressed like this nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Yeah… definitely longer than two weeks. It’s been, I don’t know, about a year and two months now, I think. That heavy depression feeling.

It kind of settled in and just… stayed. Like the low energy and the guilt, and not really wanting to eat much. I remember thinking last winter that maybe once the weather changed I’d feel different, because people always say sunlight helps, but then spring came and the trees were doing that bright green thing and I still felt the same. So… yes. Nearly every day, for a long time.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah… I have. I used to be the one doing things, you know? Like organizing rides for choir, and garden swaps—people would bring tomatoes and little pots of herbs, and someone always brought too much zucchini—and I’d help with snacks for the youth basketball games.

Now I can sit for hours just staring at my phone. Messages come in and I see them, but I don’t feel that push to answer anybody. It’s like the part of me that used to care about all that is just… not there, or it’s very far away.
Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself?

I… yeah. Not like I’m sitting there with some big plan, but the thought comes, like maybe it would be better if I just didn’t wake up. And I used to push it away harder, or not say it, because saying things makes everyone look at you differently.

But lately I don’t have the energy to fight the thought the same way. I’ve started saying it out loud at home, like, “I wish I could just not wake up,” and then everybody gets scared and quiet, and then I feel bad for scaring them. It’s not… I don’t know. It feels awful to even say here.
Do you spend a lot of time longing for your friend or feeling preoccupied with her death?

I’m… not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I think about people who’ve passed, sure, but “longing” sounds so… specific, like something you’d read on one of those pamphlets they put in the waiting room.

With my friend, I don’t know. Sometimes something reminds me of her, like a song in the grocery store or those little seasonal decorations they put out way too early, and then my mind kind of goes there. But I don’t know if I’d say I spend a lot of time on it. Time has been strange lately anyway. Some days disappear and I couldn’t tell you what I was thinking about most of the time.
During those blank moments, do you feel detached from yourself, like you’re watching yourself from the outside?

I don’t… I don’t know if it’s like watching myself from the outside. That sounds very clear, like you’d be up in the corner of the room looking down, and I don’t think I’ve noticed that exactly.

It’s more like I lose track of what I was doing. Like I’ll be holding my phone, and then the screen’s gone dark, and I’m still just sitting there. Or I’ll realize the light changed outside and I haven’t moved. But I don’t know that I feel outside my body. I’m just… not really there with things, if that makes sense.
When your mind goes blank, do those episodes happen only when your mood is very low?

No… I don’t think it was only when I was this low. Before it got really deep, I was still doing things, still getting to work, still going to church — I mean, I’d put on the vest and go stand out there like normal, and people probably thought I was fine.

But even then, for several weeks, things were already… off. I’d hear my name sometimes, and I kept thinking signs or the radio were saying things about me. Like not just a normal coincidence. And then I’d try to act regular because you don’t want people at church looking over like, “What’s wrong with her?” So… no, it wasn’t only when my mood was at the bottom.
When you heard your name or thought signs or the radio were saying things about you, did you believe those messages meant you had done something wrong or should be punished?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if the radio was saying “punishment” exactly, not like a judge reading it out loud. But it felt like… like it was pointing at me. Like I had done something wrong and everybody else somehow knew.

And then my mind goes to everything I didn’t do right. With my friend, especially. I keep replaying little things—calls I should’ve made, times I should’ve noticed something, or been better somehow. And then it spreads, you know? Like the choir, my family… even small things, like forgetting something someone asked me for, it all stacks up.

I start feeling like I’m just useless. Like I failed everybody, and if something bad is coming to me, maybe I deserve it. Which sounds awful to say out loud. But that’s where my head goes.
Do you believe you deserve to be punished?

I… yes. I mean, not in a clear way like I think someone should come and do something to me, but inside it feels like I must have earned it somehow.

I keep going over every little thing I didn’t do right — with my friend, mostly, but then it turns into the choir, my family, all of it. Like I should’ve called, or noticed, or helped more, or just been… better. And then it gets so tangled up that I feel like I’m just useless.

So when I think something bad is coming, part of me thinks… maybe that’s what I deserve.
Do you believe those signs or the radio were truly sending messages meant specifically for you?

Yes… I do. I know my sister says it’s not about me, she’ll say, “That’s just a road sign,” or “People are just talking,” but it doesn’t feel that way.

Like the city trucks, when they pass by, or the police radios — I feel like they’re keeping tabs on me. And if one of those signs flashes while I’m near it, I know it’s meant for me somehow. Even at church, if somebody lowers their voice when I walk by, I can’t shake it. It feels like they know something and they’re saying it without saying it.

I know how that sounds… but yes, it feels specific to me.

With my friend, I don’t know. Sometimes something reminds me of her, like a song in the grocery store or those little seasonal decorations they put out way too early, and then my mind kind of goes there. But I don’t know if I’d say I spend a lot of time on it. Time has been strange lately anyway. Some days disappear and I couldn’t tell you what I was thinking about most of the time.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the episodes involve dissociative detachment from self, which would help distinguish a dissociative disorder from depression, adjustment disorder, anxiety, or mild neurocognitive disorder.
doctor.question: During those blank moments, do you feel detached from yourself, like you’re watching yourself from the outside?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depersonalization or dissociation—feeling detached from oneself or watching from outside—which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles. The mention of blank moments relates contextually to concentration, but the direct focus is detachment from self.

patient.answer:
I don’t… I don’t know if it’s like watching myself from the outside. That sounds very clear, like you’d be up in the corner of the room looking down, and I don’t think I’ve noticed that exactly.

It’s more like I lose track of what I was doing. Like I’ll be holding my phone, and then the screen’s gone dark, and I’m still just sitting there. Or I’ll realize the light changed outside and I haven’t moved. But I don’t know that I feel outside my body. I’m just… not really there with things, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive syndrome is causing significant objective cognitive impairment consistent with depression rather than dissociative or adjustment-related symptoms.
doctor.question: When your mind goes blank, do those episodes happen only when your mood is very low?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: Before the depression got so deep, there were several weeks when I was still getting to work and church but already hearing my name and believing signs and radios were sending messages about me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the blank-mind/concentration episodes occur only during very low mood, which probes whether symptoms occur outside mood episodes; this most directly maps to the profile item about symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think it was only when I was this low. Before it got really deep, I was still doing things, still getting to work, still going to church — I mean, I’d put on the vest and go stand out there like normal, and people probably thought I was fine.

But even then, for several weeks, things were already… off. I’d hear my name sometimes, and I kept thinking signs or the radio were saying things about me. Like not just a normal coincidence. And then I’d try to act regular because you don’t want people at church looking over like, “What’s wrong with her?” So… no, it wasn’t only when my mood was at the bottom.

inference.note: New information suggests psychotic features outside the lowest mood states (hearing her name, ideas of reference from signs/radio), so F32.3 is added and F41.1 is dropped as primary candidate given lack of clear intense worry during blank episodes.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether psychotic symptoms are mood-congruent and present, which best distinguishes severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms from nonpsychotic depression, adjustment disorder, dissociative disorder, or organic causes.
doctor.question: When you heard your name or thought signs or the radio were saying things about you, did you believe those messages meant you had done something wrong or should be punished?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every little thing I failed to do for my friend, the choir, and my own family, and I feel like I am a useless person who deserves whatever punishment is coming.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the messages or signs were interpreted as meaning I had done something wrong or deserved punishment, which directly concerns guilt and punishment beliefs.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if the radio was saying “punishment” exactly, not like a judge reading it out loud. But it felt like… like it was pointing at me. Like I had done something wrong and everybody else somehow knew.

And then my mind goes to everything I didn’t do right. With my friend, especially. I keep replaying little things—calls I should’ve made, times I should’ve noticed something, or been better somehow. And then it spreads, you know? Like the choir, my family… even small things, like forgetting something someone asked me for, it all stacks up.

I start feeling like I’m just useless. Like I failed everybody, and if something bad is coming to me, maybe I deserve it. Which sounds awful to say out loud. But that’s where my head goes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are mood-congruent, supporting severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms over uncomplicated depression, adjustment disorder, dissociative disorder, or organic causes.
doctor.question: Do you believe you deserve to be punished?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every little thing I failed to do for my friend, the choir, and my own family, and I feel like I am a useless person who deserves whatever punishment is coming.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks directly about believing she deserves punishment, which is most directly related to excessive guilt and worthlessness.

patient.answer:
I… yes. I mean, not in a clear way like I think someone should come and do something to me, but inside it feels like I must have earned it somehow.

I keep going over every little thing I didn’t do right — with my friend, mostly, but then it turns into the choir, my family, all of it. Like I should’ve called, or noticed, or helped more, or just been… better. And then it gets so tangled up that I feel like I’m just useless.

So when I think something bad is coming, part of me thinks… maybe that’s what I deserve.

inference.note: Psychotic guilt/delusional punishment beliefs outside only low-mood episodes strongly support severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms (F32.3). Dissociative symptoms remain nonspecific without clear amnesia/depersonalization/derealization, so F44.9 stays lower. Bereavement-related adjustment remains possible but less likely given duration/severity with psychotic features. Organic mild cognitive disorder not excluded yet.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are mood-congruent delusions occurring in the context of a major depressive episode, which would support major depressive disorder with psychotic features over uncomplicated depression, adjustment disorder, dissociative disorder, or an organic mental disorder.
doctor.question: Do you believe those signs or the radio were truly sending messages meant specifically for you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I am convinced the city trucks and police radios have been keeping tabs on me, and when a road sign flashes or someone at church lowers their voice, I know it is a message about me even if my sister tells me it is not.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a fixed belief that signs or the radio were sending messages specifically meant for the patient, which directly reflects delusional ideas of reference.

patient.answer:
Yes… I do. I know my sister says it’s not about me, she’ll say, “That’s just a road sign,” or “People are just talking,” but it doesn’t feel that way.

Like the city trucks, when they pass by, or the police radios — I feel like they’re keeping tabs on me. And if one of those signs flashes while I’m near it, I know it’s meant for me somehow. Even at church, if somebody lowers their voice when I walk by, I can’t shake it. It feels like they know something and they’re saying it without saying it.

I know how that sounds… but yes, it feels specific to me.

inference.note: Psychotic features are now clearly present and mood-congruent: persecutory/reference ideas and deserved punishment alongside a sustained major depressive episode. This rules against uncomplicated F32.9, adjustment disorder, dissociative disorder, and mild organic cognitive disorder as primary explanations.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient’s main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms: persistent depressed mood for over a year, marked anhedonia, low energy, reduced appetite, excessive guilt/worthlessness, and recurrent passive death wishes. In addition, there are mood-congruent psychotic symptoms including persecutory/reference ideas and guilt/punishment beliefs (radio/signs/church voices specifically about her, being monitored, deserving punishment). Psychotic symptoms were present even before the mood worsened substantially, but the overall syndrome is still most consistent with a major depressive episode with psychotic features given the clear sustained depressive syndrome and guilt-laden, mood-congruent delusional content. Dissociative amnesia and trauma-related dissociation were not supported: she denied loss of important autobiographical information, did not clearly endorse derealization/depersonalization, and blank spells were not tied to intrusive trauma memories.
